doc.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview

chapter: Reflections on the life of a musician
title: Never being paid properly and segregated unions
summary: Ware says clubs paid nothing and left no record, and segregated locals gave musicians no protection.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Oh, the stories can go on about the things that happened to musicians. When you look back on it now and laugh, but been some mean things. Musicians, entertainers, they'd pay double. I don't care what happen, you know, you might work all night, club owner say, "Well, you ain't got no money coming Who are you gonna turn money A" (Unintelligible) tell that to?
Yeah. It seems incredible, but if can work all your life and can't prove you worked --
-- you know, you worked steady and the man's steadily taking social security out and all that, and no record of it.
You know? We have our unions and you know,

unless you working at what they call Class A clubs all your life, which isn't possible, even when they start making [segregated] locals in all the cities, across this great nation of ours, you had the dregs of the clubs. You worked all week and the cat disappears pay night and ain't nobody else supposed to come in there and play. The guy can turn his club over to his sister-in-law. You can't prove that.
It seems to me just astounding that --
